subChunks.title: Capstone Project: Build a Production-Ready Java Backend
subChunks.hookHtml: You have completed the JUNIOR tier. Advanced OOP, generics, streams, lambdas, collections, testing, REST APIs, databases, serialisation, security, logging, refactoring, Git workflows, and layered architecture — all of it converges here. Build something that demonstrates you can engineer, not just code.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What Sets This Apart From the APPRENTICE Capstone

The APPRENTICE capstone demonstrated correctness. The JUNIOR capstone demonstrates engineering judgment: layered architecture, clean API design, proper error handling, meaningful tests, and production-level concerns like logging, validation, and security basics.

Project Options

Option A: REST Task Management API

A backend REST API for managing tasks and projects. Users can create projects, add tasks with due dates and priorities, mark tasks complete, and list tasks by status. Requirements: full CRUD REST endpoints, proper status codes, request validation with meaningful error messages, JUnit 5 tests for the service layer, SLF4J logging at appropriate levels, and a layered architecture (Controller/Service/Repository pattern using interfaces).

Option B: Authentication & User Service

A user registration and login service. Users can register (username, email, password), log in to receive a JWT-style token (simulate with UUID), and access a protected endpoint only with the token. Requirements: BCrypt password hashing, no sensitive data returned in API responses, input validation, at least 5 service-layer unit tests, structured logging (no passwords in logs), and clean separation between HTTP handling and business logic.

Option C: Spell Registry API

A REST API for the Academy's spell registry. Spells have a name, tier, damage, and list of elements. The API supports search (by tier, by damage range), paginated listing, creating new spells, and an aggregate endpoint returning stats (average damage per tier, most powerful spell per element). Requirements: Jackson for request/response serialisation, stream-based aggregation in the service layer, proper REST design, request validation, JUnit tests, and logging.

Option D: Booking System

A simple appointment booking system. Resources (rooms, mages, equipment) can be booked for a time slot. The system prevents double-booking, lists available slots, and allows cancellation. Requirements: business rule enforcement in the service layer (no controller logic), at least 3 SQL queries using PreparedStatement or JPA, transaction handling for double-booking prevention, meaningful error responses, and unit tests covering booking conflict logic.

Option E: Event System

A simple event publishing and subscription system. Publishers can emit events (name, payload, timestamp). Subscribers register interest in event types and receive them when published. The system provides an API to view event history filtered by type or subscriber. Requirements: correct use of Java generics in the event model, stream-based filtering for history queries, meaningful use of functional interfaces (Predicate, Consumer), test coverage of the subscription and dispatch logic.

Mandatory Engineering Requirements

Regardless of project choice, your submission must demonstrate:

  1. Layered architecture: clear separation of Controller, Service, and Repository layers with no cross-layer violations
  2. REST design: correct HTTP methods, meaningful status codes, proper URL structure
  3. Input validation: all user-facing inputs validated before processing; informative 400 responses for invalid input
  4. Error handling: no raw stack traces in API responses; all errors return structured JSON with a message
  5. Logging: INFO for meaningful events, WARN for unexpected conditions, ERROR with context for failures
  6. Testing: at least 8 JUnit 5 test cases covering happy paths, edge cases, and validation failures
  7. Security baseline: passwords hashed (if applicable); no sensitive data in API responses or logs

storyBeats.text: The JUNIOR graduation chamber is different from the APPRENTICE hall. Where the APPRENTICE shelf held completed programs, this shelf holds deployed services — APIs with endpoints, documentation on the wall beside them, and integration test reports pinned underneath.

storyBeats.speaker: Engineering Guild Master Oryn
storyBeats.text: An APPRENTICE builds a program. A JUNIOR engineers a system. The difference is architecture: layers with clear boundaries, interfaces that allow substitution, tests that give you confidence when you change things. You have all the tools. This capstone is your proof that you know how to use them together.

storyBeats.speaker: Engineering Guild Master Oryn
storyBeats.text: When we evaluate your capstone, we look at the service layer first. That is where engineering judgment lives. Is the business logic clean and testable? Are the rules in the right place? Does the service depend on interfaces so it can be tested without a database? The controller and repository are almost mechanical — the service is where you think.

storyBeats.speaker: Engineering Guild Master Oryn
storyBeats.text: Two things will fail you immediately: raw stack traces in API responses, and no meaningful tests. A stack trace in a 500 response exposes implementation details and tells an attacker exactly where to probe. Missing tests tell us you don't yet trust your own code. Fix both before you submit.

Oryn gestures to the empty slot on the shelf. 'SENIOR tier awaits — JVM internals, concurrency, distributed systems, performance. The work you do here builds the foundation for all of it. Make the architecture clean. The SENIOR tier is unforgiving of structural debt.'

learningObjectives: Apply layered architecture across a full project with no cross-layer dependency violations
Design and implement a complete REST API with correct methods, status codes, and error responses
Write JUnit 5 tests covering the service layer including edge cases and validation failures
Apply all JUNIOR-tier skills: generics, streams, lambdas, logging, security basics, and Git workflow
commonMistakes: Putting business logic in the Controller — the service should be the smart layer
Returning raw exceptions or stack traces in API responses — always catch and return structured JSON
Writing only happy-path tests — validation failures and edge cases are where bugs live
Missing logging — especially at ERROR level with enough context to diagnose failures remotely
assessmentCriteria: The application starts and all REST endpoints respond correctly to valid inputs
Controller layer handles only HTTP concerns — no business rules, no database calls
Service layer contains all business rules and uses injected interfaces for repositories
All user inputs are validated; invalid inputs return 400 with a descriptive JSON error body
No raw stack traces in any API response — all errors are caught and mapped to structured responses
SLF4J logging present at INFO (normal flow), WARN (unexpected condition), ERROR (failures with context)
At least 8 JUnit 5 tests covering the service layer — happy paths, edge cases, validation failures
If the project involves passwords: BCrypt used, no plaintext passwords in responses or logs
subChunks.miniProject:
Extension: Production Readiness

Once your core project is working, add one or more of these production-ready features:

  • API Documentation — add Swagger/OpenAPI annotations so the API is self-documenting at /swagger-ui.html
  • Request ID Tracing — add a request ID to every request's MDC at the entry point and include it in all log lines and error responses
  • Rate Limiting — implement a simple in-memory rate limiter (e.g. max 10 requests per minute per IP) using a Map and timestamps
  • Pagination — add offset/limit pagination to any list endpoint and return total count in the response headers
  • Integration Tests — write at least 3 tests that call the REST endpoints directly (using Spring's MockMvc or TestRestTemplate) rather than testing the service layer in isolation
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Describe your completed JUNIOR capstone as if presenting it in a technical interview. Walk through the architecture diagram you'd draw on a whiteboard. Explain your service layer's design decisions. What would you do differently if you had more time? What was the hardest engineering decision you made?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Architecture planning exercise — complete this before writing any code:

  1. Name your chosen project option (A through E)
  2. Draw or describe the class diagram: list every class/interface, which layer it belongs to, and its primary responsibility
  3. Identify your two most complex business rules and describe how you will test each in the service layer (method name, input, expected outcome)
  4. List three API endpoints with method, URL, request body, and expected status codes for success and validation failure
  5. Identify one place where security matters in your chosen project and describe your approach
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Example plan for Option A (Task Management API):

1. Project: REST Task Management API

2. Class diagram:
   TaskController (Presentation) — handles HTTP, delegates to TaskService
   TaskService (Business Logic) — validates, enforces business rules, calls TaskRepository
   TaskRepository interface (Data Access boundary)
   InMemoryTaskRepository implements TaskRepository (simple in-memory store for this project)
   Task domain object — id, title, dueDate, priority, status, projectId
   Project domain object — id, name, ownerId
   ApiError (shared) — structured error response DTO

3. Two complex business rules:
   a. Cannot create a task with a past due date
      → Test: createTask_pastDueDate_throwsIllegalArgumentException
      Input: Task with dueDate = yesterday
      Expected: IllegalArgumentException("Due date must be in the future")
   b. Completing a task requires the task to exist and belong to the requesting project
      → Test: completeTask_taskNotInProject_throwsNotFoundException
      Input: taskId from project A, projectId = project B
      Expected: NotFoundException("Task not found in project")

4. Three endpoints:
   POST /api/projects/{projectId}/tasks
     Body: {"title":"Build API","priority":"HIGH","dueDate":"2026-06-01"}
     Success: 201 Created + task JSON
     Validation failure: 400 + {"error":"Title must not be blank"}

   PATCH /api/tasks/{taskId}/complete
     Body: none
     Success: 200 OK + updated task
     Not found: 404 + {"error":"Task not found"}

   GET /api/projects/{projectId}/tasks?status=PENDING
     Success: 200 + JSON array of tasks

5. Security concern: task ownership — a user must not be able to complete or view another user's tasks.
   Approach: add userId to all requests (via header or path param), validate in service layer that the task's projectId belongs to the requesting userId before any mutation.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Build your chosen capstone project. When complete, save it to your profile using the 'Save Project' button above. Your submission should include:

  • Full source code (paste or link to GitHub repository)
  • A brief architecture description (2–3 sentences per layer)
  • A list of all REST endpoints with their expected status codes
  • A summary of your test cases and their results
  • One paragraph describing the most complex business rule you implemented and how you tested it

Your submission will be reviewed against the 8 mandatory engineering requirements listed in this lesson.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
A strong JUNIOR capstone submission demonstrates:

✅ Three-layer architecture visible in package/class structure — no business logic in Controllers
✅ Service layer with injected repository interface — mockable in tests without a real database
✅ REST endpoints returning correct status codes: 200/201 for success, 400 for validation, 404 for not found, 500 for unexpected errors
✅ All validation in the service layer: checked before any database operation
✅ Structured error responses: {"error": "descriptive message"} on all 4xx/5xx responses
✅ SLF4J logging: at least one INFO per successful operation, WARN for unusual conditions, ERROR with the exception for failures
✅ 8+ JUnit 5 tests: at least 3 happy paths, at least 3 validation failures, at least 2 edge cases
✅ Security: passwords BCrypt-hashed (if auth involved), no plaintext in logs or responses

What reviewers look for in the service layer:
- Business rules are methods with clear names (not anonymous if/else blocks)
- No HTTP types (HttpServletRequest, ResponseEntity) in the service
- No new Repository() instantiation — constructor injection only
- Exception types match the scenario: IllegalArgumentException for validation, ResourceNotFoundException for 404 scenarios

questions.questionHtml: A REST endpoint receives an invalid request body (missing required field). Which status code should it return?
questions.explanationHtml: 400 Bad Request signals that the request was syntactically or semantically invalid — the client's fault. The response body should include a descriptive error message explaining what was wrong and how to fix it.

questions.questionHtml: Which testing approach best validates the service layer in isolation?
options: Start the full application and send real HTTP requests
Use a real database populated with test data
Inject mock implementations of repositories and verify method calls and return values
Copy the service logic into a separate test class and test it there
questions.correctAnswer: Inject mock implementations of repositories and verify method calls and return values
questions.explanationHtml: Service layer unit tests should inject mock (or stub) repositories. This avoids database setup, makes tests fast and deterministic, and proves the service works correctly regardless of what the repository returns. Use Mockito in a real JUnit test, or hand-roll simple stubs as you've done in the APPRENTICE tier.

questions.questionHtml: A developer's REST endpoint throws an unhandled exception when the database is unreachable. What does the client receive by default in a Spring Boot application?
options: A 500 Internal Server Error with the full stack trace in the response body
questions.correctAnswer: A 500 Internal Server Error with the full stack trace in the response body
questions.explanationHtml: By default, Spring Boot's error handling returns a 500 with a JSON error body that may include the stack trace (especially in development mode). This exposes implementation details to clients. Always implement a global exception handler (@ControllerAdvice) to catch exceptions and return structured, safe error responses.
